title: [Chapitre] III. Réseaux via découpages : notes manuscrites (08/06/1986).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting. Chapter III ('Réseaux via découpages') studies 'tronçons', ordered segments with origin or(L) and extremity ex(L), together with their sub-intervals. Pages 22-23 digress to ask which topology a general lattice L should carry. Page 22 had a 'canonical' topology, apparently a one-sided (Alexandrov-type, lower or upper) topology. It is T0, but points and segments [a,b] are not closed in it unless L is totally ordered. Page 22 therefore introduced a second topology whose closed sets are generated by [a,b], L_{>=a} and L_{<=a}. This is essentially Frink's interval topology, since [a,b] = L_{>=a} ∩ L_{<=a}.

Page 23. The trouble is that in this interval topology the open interval ]a,b[ 'no longer wants to be open'. When L is totally ordered, the complement of ]a,b[ is L_{<=a} ∪ L_{>=b}, which is closed, so there is no problem. For a non-total lattice the complement of ]a,b[ is not a finite union of basic closed sets.

Grothendieck's remedy is the least topology finer than both natural candidates (the supremum of the two topologies). Its open subbasis is:
- L_{<a}, L_{>a} and ]a,b[ for a<b;
- the complements of L_{>=a}, of L_{<=a} and of [a,b] for a<=b.

He then asks whether the expected closure formulas hold:
- closure(]a,b[) = [a,b];
- closure(L_{<a}) = L_{<=a} when a is not the least element 0_L;
- closure(L_{>a}) = L_{>=a} when a is not the greatest element.

To get a ∈ closure(]a,b[) it would suffice that every elementary open set (a finite intersection of subbasic opens) containing a contains some ]a,ε[ with a<ε<b. He asserts this already fails for a lattice coming from a topological situation. The marginal sketch is a hatched diagonal strip with points x, a, b, y. The proposed counterexample is an elementary open set ∁[x,y] that contains a while ]a,b[ ⊂ [x,y].

Outcome. Page 24 abandons this refinement: 'on travaillera avec la top. définie d'abord' (the interval-closed topology). The closed intervals [a,b], L_{<=a}, L_{>=a} are then called closed sub-tronçons. For the totally ordered tronçons the chapter really concerns, all candidate topologies coincide with the order topology, so the digression is harmless.
errors: The opening worry ('ouvert ennuyé') concerns only non-totally-ordered lattices. For a totally ordered L, ]a,b[ is open in the interval-closed topology, and that topology is just the order topology.

The marginal counterexample is too sketchy to verify, and it is not clear it works as stated. For the product order on R^2, suppose ]a,b[ ⊂ [x,y]. Then x <= z for all z in ]a,b[ and, z tending to a, x <= a; similarly a <= y because the order is closed. Hence a ∈ [x,y], which contradicts the claim. Some other lattice, perhaps the strip in the sketch, or a non-dense ('jumping') order would be needed.
'La moins fine des deux' should presumably read the least topology finer than both (their supremum). The coarser of the two would not contain all the listed opens.

The sufficient condition stated (every elementary open containing a contains some ]a,ε[) is stronger than what is needed. It is enough that every elementary open containing a meets ]a,b[, and that condition could hold even when the stronger one fails.

ideas.what: Closed subbasis of principal up-sets and down-sets (with intervals [a,b]) on a lattice, making points and intervals closed
ideas.usually_credited_to: O. Frink (1942); G. Birkhoff, Lattice Theory

ideas.what: Topology generated by open intervals and open rays L_{<a}, L_{>a}
Supremum of the two topologies, and the question whether closure(]a,b[) = [a,b] and closure of open rays = closed rays
ideas.modern_name: Join of order-compatible topologies; density of open intervals / order-density conditions
ideas.usually_credited_to: folklore in ordered topological spaces (Nachbin, Ward, etc.)

deep.surprise_reason: This is an exploratory digression on elementary topologies on lattices (interval topology versus order topology), which is classical material. Grothendieck himself abandons it on the next page and works with the interval-closed topology on totally ordered tronçons. Nothing here is new beyond showing his working process in the 1986 'tronçons/découpages' material.
transcription_corrections: Open subbasis line: the complement sign ∁ applies to [a,b] as well, i.e. ∁L_{>=a}, ∁L_{<=a}, ∁[a,b] (a<=b). The set [a,b] itself is not open.
'la topologie la moins fine des deux' likely means the least topology finer than both (supremum of the two topologies); wording uncertain.
Margin: the figure is a hatched diagonal strip with x, a, b, y marked, and the text reads roughly 'Si ... a ∈ ∁[x,y] mais ]a,b[ ⊂ [x,y]'.

'un ens. de base associé à un treillis topologique' is uncertain. It possibly refers to an ordered set or lattice arising from a topological (geometric) situation, i.e. the strip pictured in the margin.
